passage:
On the third night, Vikas and Salma were still in the small office above the hardware shop in town, sending emails. The one deck, unchanged, went to every investor address they could find, two hundred of them. Salma pasted names until the tea went cold.
The replies came fast and short. "Thanks, but we only back financial apps." "Not our area." "We don't invest at this stage." Some were kind, most were automatic.
By the end of the week they had spent long hours and had not one meeting. Vikas stared at the screen, thinking each no meant the idea was bad, when many just said the fund was the wrong one. Salma closed the laptop and said nothing.

qa.q: Where were Vikas and Salma sending the emails from?
qa.a: They sent them from the small office above the hardware shop in town.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling while reading the replies?
qa.a: Vikas was discouraged, taking each no as proof the idea was weak, which is why the screen was hard to look away from.

qa.q: What could Vikas and Salma try instead of another mass email?
qa.a: They could research a short list of investors who back businesses like theirs and write to each about why they fit.

qa.q: How might an investor see a deck sent to everyone?
qa.a: An investor sees a message that ignores their focus, so a quick no from a fund that backs something else is the natural reply.

grounding: The passage shows a founder sending the same deck to hundreds of investors without research, getting fast rejections and wasting the team's time.

passage:
Rafael was sure it was a numbers game. From their tiny office in Porto, he and Beatriz built a spreadsheet of two hundred investor emails gathered from websites and old event lists, and sent every one the same deck about their restaurant-booking app, with "Dear Investor" at the top.
It took four evenings. Beatriz wanted to check who actually invested in restaurants or consumer apps. "No time," Rafael said. "Volume."
Within a week the replies began. "We only invest in medical devices." "We don't do consumer." "We're a later-stage fund." Most never replied at all. By the end of the month they had one meeting, with an investor who spent the first ten minutes explaining that he focused on farming technology.
Beatriz added up the hours: about thirty, gone. Their app hadn't been touched in two weeks.

qa.q: How many investors did they email?
What was Rafael feeling when he said "Volume"?
qa.a: Rafael was eager and impatient, believing more emails meant better odds and that research would waste time.

qa.q: What could they have done instead of mass emailing?
qa.a: Picked a smaller list of investors who back restaurant or consumer apps and written to each one properly.

qa.q: How does Beatriz see the result?
qa.a: Beatriz sees about thirty hours wasted and the app untouched, which likely frustrates her after she had wanted to check fit.

grounding: It shows founders sending the same deck to two hundred investors without research, so most reject them as outside their focus and the team's time is wasted.

passage:
At the university incubator, Nazia had claimed the corner desk and a stack of printouts. Her plan: email the same pitch deck for her farm-drone startup to every investor in the incubator's database, all two hundred of them, before Friday.
Akash, the incubator manager, stopped by on Tuesday. "Have you checked which of them invest in agriculture?"
"It's faster to send to everyone. Someone will bite."
Two weeks later Nazia sat in Akash's office with her inbox open. Thirty-one replies, twenty-eight of them polite no's: "Outside our focus." "We only do fintech." "Too early for us." Three asked for calls; two of those were later-stage funds that dropped out after the first question. Her team had paused the field trial for a week to send and track all that email.
Akash pulled up a chair. "Now let's find the twenty who actually fund farm tech."

qa.q: How many replies did Nazia get?
qa.a: Thirty-one, twenty-eight of them polite no's.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling as she sat in Akash's office with her inbox open?
qa.a: Nazia was probably discouraged and a bit embarrassed after the rejections and the lost week.

qa.q: What is Akash's suggestion, and why is it better?
qa.a: Finding the twenty investors who actually fund farm technology, because focused pitches match their interests and save time.

qa.q: How was Nazia's team affected by the mass emailing?
qa.a: The team paused the field trial for a week to send and track emails, delaying real product work.

grounding: It shows a founder emailing the same deck to two hundred investors without checking their focus, getting mostly rejections and losing the team's time.
